newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak c.bank supports subordinated debt issues. [CORRECTED 16:47 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Slovak c.bank supports subordinated debt issues. [CORRECTED 16:47 GMT]

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) said on Friday it supports attempts by the country's two largest commercial banks to issue subordinated debt abroad to help boost their capital.
The banks Slovenska Sporitelna a.s. and credit bank Vseobecna Uverova Banka a.s. (VUB), announced over the past month their plans to launch the first subordinated debt in central Europe.
NBS vice-governor Jozef Mudrik told Reuters in an interview he hoped the two banks would succeed in their ongoing negotiations, which he suggested could be tough.
"This form should be good (for the banks) in this situation when the extent of a state budget contribution to bank loan portfolio restructuring is (still) a question," Mudrik said.

But he added that similar talks held with the World Bank a few years ago, when it offered Slovakia to help loan portfolio restructuring in its three largest banks via a subordinated debt "did not end positively".
"The reasons why the offer was not approved, I think, were other than economical," Mudrik said.
The Slovak government has been preparing for over a year on plans for tax deductions and for provisioning regulations on classified (corrects from "subordinated") debt.
But the government still taxes provisions for country's classified loans, of which some 90 percent is extended by Sporitelna, VUB and IRB Bank.
The three banks are still majority-owned by state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund (NPF).
To maintain if not improve their below standard capital adequacy ratio without changing bank ownership, Sporitelna and VUB said they were forced to the subordinated debt option.
Both banks have said the issue was "highly delicate", but would not specify further.
"Subordinated debt would disburden the state budget...but it is extended under no conditions from the creditor's side," said Mudrik.
"Plus if a bank happens to go bankrupt this kind of debt is the last to be repayed, and this is a problem".
Mudrik added that "of course it is difficult to find the institution which would provide subordinated debt under such conditions." -- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-563-3687
